Not assumed: monomer, polymer, addition polymerisation, initiator, repeat unit, backbone, side group, thermoplastic, plasticiser, LDPE, HDPE, PVC, PS, PTFE.
progression.startsWith: Open the alkene double bond. The video opens: Ethene is a gas. Join thousands of ethene molecules end to end, and you get polyethylene, a solid tough enough for bags and milk bottles. Swap one hydrogen on each ethene for a chlorine, and you get the plastic in grey PVC water pipes.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining addition polymerisation; drawing a repeat unit with brackets, n and continuation bonds; recovering the monomer from a repeat unit; explaining why polyethylene is a solid and a thermoplastic; comparing LDPE and HDPE by branching; explaining the properties and uses of PVC, PS and PTFE from their side groups. teaching.task: Ethene is a gas, yet thousands of ethene molecules joined together make a solid plastic. How does an alkene become an addition polymer, and why do plastics from such similar monomers, like PE, PVC, PS and PTFE, behave so differently?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a gas of two-carbon molecules becomes a solid plastic, and similar monomers give very different plastics (1); (2) the C=C's weaker second bond breaks, each carbon's spare bond joins the next monomer, again and again, and nothing else forms (2); (3) one repeat unit: single bond, continuation bonds, brackets, n; the double-bond carbons form the backbone and the rest hangs off (3); (4) backwards: restore the C=C, add no hydrogens (4); (5) very long chains lie alongside each other, so dispersion forces along the whole contact make a solid; no bonds join one chain to another; heat lets chains slide, so it softens and remoulds without breaking chain bonds (thermoplastic) (5); (6) branches stop packing, so less contact, weaker forces: LDPE soft and lower melting; straight chains pack: HDPE stiff and denser (6); (7) polar C–Cl adds dipole–dipole: rigid PVC; plasticisers push chains apart (7); (8) bulky, stiff rings catch on neighbouring chains and stop them sliding: rigid, brittle PS; gas-filled foam insulates (8); (9) strong C–F bonds and a fluorine sheath resist attack; the even sheath cancels the C–F pulls and tightly held electrons hardly shift, so only weak dispersion forces form at the surface and almost nothing sticks: PTFE (9); memory aid and comparison (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: ethene is a gas, yet thousands of ethene molecules joined end to end make polyethylene, a solid tough enough for bags and bottles, and similar monomers give very different plastics, so the video asks how an alkene becomes an addition polymer and why PE, PVC, PS and PTFE behave so differently. A monomer joins up into a polymer: the C=C's weaker second bond breaks, each carbon's spare bond joins the next monomer, again and again, and nothing else is formed. The repeat unit is drawn once with the double bond as a single bond, continuation bonds through brackets and an n, and the monomer is found by going backwards. Polyethylene is solid because each huge chain lies alongside its neighbours for thousands of carbons, so the dispersion forces add up, and it softens on heating because no covalent bonds join the chains. LDPE's short branches keep chains apart, so it is soft and flexible, while HDPE's straight chains pack closely and make it stiff. In PVC the polar carbon-chlorine bond adds dipole attractions between chains, polystyrene's bulky rings stop chains sliding past each other so it is rigid, and in PTFE strong carbon-fluorine bonds and a fluorine sheath make it unreactive and non-stick. The memory aid is open the double bond, add brackets, nothing lost, and each property is traced back to the chains. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Ethene is a gas. Join thousands of ethene molecules end to end, and you get polyethylene, a solid tough enough for bags and milk bottles. Swap one hydrogen on each ethene for a chlorine, and you get the plastic in grey PVC water pipes. So how does an alkene turn into a solid like this, and why do plastics made from such similar molecules behave so differently?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "(a) 1,1-Dichloroethene, CH₂=CCl₂, forms an addition polymer. Draw the repeat unit of this polymer. (b) Another addition polymer has the repeat unit shown. Name and draw its monomer." with the repeat unit [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ drawn in plain ink on the card. New monomer in (a) (scenes use chloroethene; both chlorines on one carbon tests "everything else hangs off"); (b) tests monomer recovery. Crossed mistake: "monomer: CH₃–CH₂–CH₃" (hydrogens added at the continuation bonds; site correction 1). (A2) "High-density polyethylene (HDPE) is used for rigid chopping boards, and low-density polyethylene (LDPE) is used for soft squeeze bottles. Both are made from ethene. Explain how differences in chain structure lead to these different properties, and explain why both can be melted and remoulded for recycling." New context (site uses milk crates and cling film); tests branching, packing, contact, dispersion forces and thermoplastic behaviour. Crossed mistake: "Melting breaks the covalent bonds in the chains." (pack trap: chain movement, not chain breaking).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "model and compare the structure, properties and uses of addition polymers of ethylene and related monomers, for example:; polyethylene (PE); polyvinyl chloride (PVC); polystyrene (PS); polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) (ACSCH136)" This video covers how addition polymerisation opens the C=C bond, drawing a repeat unit from a monomer and a monomer from a repeat unit, why the chains form a solid that softens on heating (thermoplastic behaviour), and how branching (LDPE against HDPE) and side groups (PVC, PS, PTFE) set properties and uses. Condensation polymers are chem-m7-c15; the polymer practice video is chem-m7-g04 (route review change 4). this video starts by opening the alkene double bond, and stops at linking repeat-unit structure to properties and uses. It teaches: a monomer is a small molecule that joins into a long chain, the polymer (many parts); in addition polymerisation the weaker second bond of each C=C breaks (c04a), leaving each carbon one spare bond, which joins it to the next monomer; an initiator opens the first double bond and each new chain end opens the next (one sentence, no mechanism); nothing else forms, so every monomer atom ends up in the chain; the repeat unit: the monomer redrawn with a single bond, a continuation bond out of each backbone carbon, square brackets crossed by those bonds, and n outside; the two carbons from the double bond form the backbone and everything else hangs off as a side group; the equation n CH₂=CHCl → [–CH₂–CHCl–]ₙ; going backwards: take the two backbone carbons, remove the continuation bonds and restore the C=C, adding no hydrogens; the chains are very long and lie alongside each other, so dispersion forces acting along the whole contact hold them together and the polymer is a solid; heating lets the chains move and slide past each other, so the plastic softens and can be remoulded, and cooling restores the forces; the covalent bonds in the chains do not break; this is a thermoplastic, which is what makes melt recycling possible; no bonds join one chain to another, only these forces (Revision 2); LDPE and HDPE share the monomer and repeat unit but differ in branching (made under different conditions): branches stop chains packing closely, so less contact, weaker dispersion forces, lower density, softer, lower melting (about 110 °C; squeeze bottles, films); straight chains pack closely with neatly lined-up regions, so more contact, stronger forces, higher density, stiffer, higher melting (about 130 °C; crates, milk bottles); PVC: the polar C–Cl bond adds dipole–dipole attraction between chains, so plain PVC is rigid (pipes); plasticisers between the chains push them apart and make it flexible (cable coating); polystyrene: the bulky, stiff benzene ring on every second carbon catches on the rings of neighbouring chains, so at room temperature the chains can hardly slide, and it is rigid and brittle (Revision 2: the cause is restricted sliding, not poor packing, which scene 6 links to softness); blown with gas it becomes a light insulating foam (cups); PTFE: every H replaced by F; C–F bonds are among the strongest single bonds carbon forms and the F atoms wrap the backbone, so very few chemicals attack it (chemical resistance comes from these bonds, not from forces between chains); C–F bonds are polar, but the even fluorine coating makes their pulls largely cancel, and fluorine holds its electrons so tightly that they hardly shift, so other substances make only very weak dispersion forces with the surface (c03), so almost nothing sticks (non-stick pans, plumber's tape). Not here: condensation polymers, PET and nylon (chem-m7-c15; the PET bottle in the hook plate gets a grey forward tag); polymerisation conditions and the radical mechanism (initiation, propagation, termination by name; author note a); tacticity and crystallinity numbers (author note b); thermosets beyond one grey chip (site L23 extension; author note c); environmental persistence, microplastics, recycling codes and bioplastics (site L21 card 4 and L23, beyond the 2017 dotpoints; route review change 4; author note d); natural polymers and hydrolysis of biomolecules (site L23 card 8, not a 2017 Module 7 dotpoint; site correction 6); bond energy calculations; polypropylene and polyacrylonitrile as taught examples (propene appears only as attempt 1's monomer; author note e).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c04a and c03: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; the C=C teal, its second bond shown as a teal cloud when it opens; chlorine green; fluorine pale green-yellow; the benzene ring ink with a grey ring; brackets and n in navy; chains in the chain view pale blue; dispersion contact dotted pale blue; dipole–dipole dotted teal with δ+ and δ− small in navy; heat glow amber. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Monomer to polymer", "Draw it", "Backwards", "Why solid?", "LDPE or HDPE", "Side groups"); centre the structure board or the chain view box, one model at a time; plates small or medium at the left or right only in scenes 1, 6 to 9, 14 and 15. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous model leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 27 Oct): `m7-polymer-objects-v1.png` (2000 × 2000; a white plastic carry bag, a grey pipe with a coupling, a white foam cup, a clear blue-tinted drink bottle and a coil of cream rope; scenes 1 and 15, medium). Not used: `m6-foam-cup-calorimeter-v1.png` (a foam cup with a lid, thermometer and cutaway water; it reads as calorimetry apparatus, not a polystyrene object); `m6-household-cleaner-bottle-v1.png` (a spray bottle of unknown polymer). Five new plates (Assets). All plates scaled uniformly only, never stretched. No human figures.
